pages.title: Standard Input in Node.js with fs.readFileSync(0)
pages.content:
# Synchronous Standard Input in Node.js

In competitive programming and coding assessment platforms (like HackerRank, LeetCode, and SEED-IT), reading the entire input synchronously from standard input (`stdin`, file descriptor `0`) is the fastest and most reliable approach:

```javascript
const fs = require('fs');
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf-8');
```

### How It Works
- `0` represents the standard input stream file descriptor in Unix and Windows.
- `'utf-8'` specifies string encoding rather than a raw buffer.
- It reads all input up to EOF (End-of-File) into memory in a single fast operation.

callout.title: File Descriptor 0
callout.text: Using fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf-8') avoids asynchronous event buffering overhead and guarantees all test input is present before execution proceeds.

checkpoint.question: Which file descriptor number represents standard input (stdin) in fs.readFileSync()?
checkpoint.explanation: File descriptor 0 is standard input (stdin). 1 is stdout, and 2 is stderr.

pages.title: Parsing Line-by-Line Input with the readline Module

callout.title: When to Use readline vs readFileSync
callout.text: Use readline for interactive CLI prompts and memory-constrained streams. Use readFileSync(0) for competitive programming problem solving.

checkpoint.question: Which event does the readline interface emit whenever a new line is entered?
checkpoint.explanation: The readline interface emits the 'line' event whenever the input stream receives an end-of-line marker.

pages.title: Processing Numeric and Multi-Line Problem Inputs

callout.title: Using /\s+/ for Splitting
callout.text: Always split with the regex /\s+/ instead of ' '. This handles multiple consecutive spaces, tabs, and Windows carriage returns (\r\n) cleanly.

checkpoint.question: Why is split(/\s+/) preferred over split(' ') when parsing competitive programming inputs?
options: It correctly handles multiple consecutive spaces, tabs, and newlines without creating empty string tokens
split(' ') does not support ASCII numbers
Regex splitting is mandatory in strict mode
checkpoint.explanation: The regular expression /\s+/ matches one or more consecutive whitespace characters (including tabs and newlines), avoiding accidental empty tokens.

pages.title: Handling Input Delimiters, Whitespace, and Stream EOF
pages.content:
# Defensive Input Handling and Edge Cases

Real-world inputs frequently contain trailing blank lines, carriage returns from Windows systems (`\r`), or leading whitespace:

### Best Practices
- **Always `.trim()` raw input**: Strips trailing newlines that might produce empty array items when calling `.split('\n')`.
- **Handle Empty Lines**: Filter out blank lines using `.filter(Boolean)` or `.filter(line => line.length > 0)`.
- **Radix in parseInt**: Always specify radix 10: `parseInt(val, 10)` to prevent unexpected octal parsing.

```javascript
const cleanLines = input.trim().split('\n').map(l => l.trim()).filter(Boolean);
```

callout.title: Watch Out for \r (Carriage Return)
callout.text: Windows-encoded inputs contain \r\n. Calling split('\n') can leave trailing \r on lines. Using line.trim() removes \r cleanly.

checkpoint.question: Why should you always supply radix 10 when calling parseInt(str, 10)?
options: To ensure numbers are always parsed in base 10 (decimal), avoiding historical octal/hex misinterpretations
Because parseInt throws an exception without a second argument
To convert negative numbers to positive
checkpoint.explanation: Passing radix 10 explicitly guarantees base-10 decimal conversion, preventing strings with leading zeros from being parsed as octal.

questions.question: Which synchronous Node.js function reads the entirety of standard input from file descriptor 0?
questions.explanation: fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf-8') reads all data from standard input (fd 0) as a UTF-8 string synchronously.

questions.question: Which Node.js core module provides a streaming interface for reading data line-by-line?
questions.explanation: The readline module provides an interface for reading data from a Readable stream line by line.

questions.question: How do you split a space-separated string of numbers '10 20 30' into an array of number primitives?
questions.explanation: str.split(' ').map(Number) splits into substring tokens and passes each token to Number constructor.

questions.question: What does the second argument (radix) in parseInt(str, radix) specify?
options: The mathematical base of the number system (e.g. 10 for decimal, 16 for hexadecimal)
questions.explanation: The radix parameter specifies the base of the numeral system to be used.

questions.question: What does trim() do before splitting an input string?
options: Removes leading and trailing whitespace characters including newlines
Deletes all spaces throughout the entire string
questions.explanation: trim() strips leading and trailing whitespace, preventing extra empty tokens from trailing newlines.

questions.question: What does parseInt('100px', 10) return?
questions.explanation: parseInt parses leading valid numeric characters until encountering an invalid character ('p'), returning 100.

questions.question: What does Number('100px') return in contrast to parseInt?
questions.explanation: Number('100px') requires the entire string to be numeric; if non-numeric characters exist, it returns NaN.

questions.question: How can you read arguments passed to a Node.js script via command-line (e.g. node app.js foo bar)?
questions.explanation: process.argv is an array containing the command-line arguments passed when launching the Node.js process.

questions.question: In browser JavaScript, which function prompts the user to enter text via a modal dialog?
questions.explanation: prompt() displays a browser modal dialog asking the user to enter text, returning the string or null if cancelled.

questions.question: What is the result of Number(null) and Number(undefined)?
questions.explanation: In JavaScript type conversion, Number(null) evaluates to 0, whereas Number(undefined) evaluates to NaN.
